title: Chapter 8 — The Federal Constitution
paragraphs: Until now I have treated each State as a separate whole, and I have explained the various springs the people sets in motion and the various means of action it uses. But all the States I have treated as independent must, in certain cases, submit to the supreme authority of the Union. The time has now come to examine separately the supremacy the Union has been given, and to take a quick look at the Federal Constitution.
Origin of the first Union — Its weakness — Congress appeals to the constituent authority — Two years pass between this appeal and the announcement of the new Constitution.
History of the Federal Constitution

The thirteen colonies that threw off the English yoke at the same moment, toward the end of the last century, had, as I have already observed, the same religion, the same language, the same customs, and almost the same laws. They were fighting a common enemy. These reasons were strong enough to unite them with one another and to consolidate them into one nation. But each colony had enjoyed a separate existence and a government under its own control, and the particular interests and customs that this system produced stood against a close and intimate union, which would have absorbed the individual importance of each into the general importance of all. Hence two opposite tendencies arose: one urged the Anglo-Americans to unite, the other to divide their strength. As long as the war with the mother country lasted, necessity kept the principle of union alive. The laws that established it were defective, yet the common tie held in spite of their flaws. *a But as soon as peace was concluded, the faults of the legislation became obvious, and the State seemed to dissolve all at once. Each colony became an independent republic and claimed absolute sovereignty. The Federal government had been condemned to impotence by its constitution, and a common danger no longer supported it. It witnessed the outrages offered to its flag by the great nations of Europe, and it could scarcely hold its ground against the Native American tribes or pay the interest on the debt contracted during the war of independence. It was already on the verge of collapse when it officially declared that it could not govern and appealed to the constituent authority of the nation. *b If America ever came near (however briefly) to that lofty pinnacle of glory to which its inhabitants like to point in their imagination, it was at the solemn moment when the power of the nation, so to speak, gave up its rule over the land. Every age has offered the spectacle of a people struggling vigorously to win its independence, and the efforts of the Americans in throwing off the English yoke have been greatly exaggerated. They were separated from their enemies by three thousand miles of ocean and backed by a powerful ally. The success of the United States may more fairly be credited to their geographical position than to the valor of their armies or the patriotism of their citizens. It would be ridiculous to compare the American war with the wars of the French Revolution, or the efforts of the Americans with those of the French. The French were attacked by the whole of Europe, without credit and without allies, and yet they were able to set a twentieth part of their population against the world, and to carry the torch of revolution beyond their frontiers while they smothered its devouring flame at home. But it is a novelty in the history of society to see a great people turn a calm and searching eye on itself when the legislature informs it that the wheels of government have stopped. It examines the extent of the evil with care and waits patiently for two whole years until a remedy is found, and it then adopts that remedy of its own free will, without having wrung a tear or a drop of blood from mankind. When the inadequacy of the first constitution was discovered, America had a double advantage: the calm that had followed the excitement of the revolution, and the great men who had led the revolution to a successful end. The assembly that took on the task of composing the second constitution was small, *c but George Washington was its President, and it held the finest talents and the noblest hearts the New World had ever produced. After long and careful deliberation, this national commission offered the people the body of general laws that still governs the Union. All the States adopted it one after another. *d The new Federal government began its functions in 1789, after an interregnum of two years. The American Revolution ended when the French Revolution began.

a [ See the articles of the first confederation formed in 1778. This constitution was not adopted by all the States until 1781. See also the analysis given of this constitution in “The Federalist” from No. 15 to No. 22, inclusive, and Story’s “Commentaries on the Constitution of the United States,” pp. 85-115.]
b [ Congress made this declaration on February 21, 1787.]
c [ It consisted of fifty-five members; Washington, Madison, Hamilton, and the two Morrises were among them.]

d [ It was not adopted by the legislative bodies. Instead, representatives were elected by the people for this one purpose, and the new constitution was discussed at length in each of these assemblies.]
Summary of the Federal Constitution
Division of authority between the Federal government and the States — The government of the States is the rule, the Federal government the exception.

The first question facing the Americans was intricate and by no means easy to solve. The aim was to divide the authority of the different States that made up the Union in such a way that each State would keep governing itself in everything that concerned its internal prosperity, while the entire nation, represented by the Union, would keep forming a compact body and would provide for the general needs of the people. It was as impossible to determine in advance, with any accuracy, the share of authority each of two governments would have as it was to foresee every incident in the life of a nation.

The obligations and claims of the Federal government were simple and easy to define, because the Union had been formed expressly to meet the general needs of the people. The claims and obligations of the States, on the other hand, were complicated and varied, because their governments had reached into every detail of social life. The powers of the Federal government were therefore carefully listed, and everything not included among them was declared to belong to the privileges of the several State governments. Thus the government of the States remained the rule, and that of the Confederation became the exception. *e
e [ See the Amendment to the Federal Constitution; “Federalist,” No. 32; Story, p. 711; Kent’s “Commentaries,” vol. i. p. 364.

It should be observed that whenever the Constitution does not reserve to Congress the exclusive right to regulate certain matters, the States may take up the matter until it is brought before the National Assembly. For instance, Congress has the right to make a general law on bankruptcy, but it neglects to do so. Each State is then free to make a law for itself. This point has been settled by argument in the law courts, and it may be said to belong more properly to jurisprudence.]

But it was foreseen that in practice questions might arise about the exact limits of this exceptional authority, and that it would be dangerous to submit such questions to the ordinary courts of justice, which the States themselves had set up in the States. A high Federal court was therefore created, *f whose purpose, among other functions, was to maintain the balance of power the Constitution had established between the two rival governments. *g
f [ The action of this court is indirect, as we shall show later.]

g [ This is how “The Federalist,” No. 45, explains the division of supremacy between the Union and the States: “The powers delegated by the Constitution to the Federal Government are few and defined. Those which are to remain in the State Governments are numerous and indefinite. The former will be exercised principally on external objects, as war, peace, negotiation, and foreign commerce. The powers reserved to the several States will extend to all the objects which, in the ordinary course of affairs, concern the internal order and prosperity of the State.” I shall often have occasion to quote “The Federalist” in this work. When the bill that has since become the Constitution of the United States was submitted to the people for approval, and the discussions were still going on, three men formed an association to explain to the nation the advantages of the proposed measure. They had already won a share of the fame they have enjoyed since: John Jay, Hamilton, and Madison. To this end they published a series of articles in the form of a journal, and the articles now make up a complete treatise. They called their journal “The Federalist,” and the name has stayed with the work. “The Federalist” is an excellent book, which ought to be familiar to the statesmen of every country, although it concerns America in particular.]
Prerogative of the Federal Government

The power to declare war, make peace, and levy general taxes belongs to the Federal government — What part of the country’s internal policy it may direct — In some respects the government of the Union is more centralized than the King’s government in the old French monarchy.

A people’s external relations can be compared to those of private individuals, and they cannot be managed well without a single head of government. The Union was therefore given the exclusive right to make peace and war, to conclude commercial treaties, to raise armies, and to equip fleets. *h The need for a national government was felt less urgently in directing the internal policy of society, but there are certain general interests that only a general authority can serve well. The Union was given the power to control the monetary system, to run the post office, and to open the great roads that were to connect the different parts of the country. *i The independence of each State’s government within its own sphere was formally recognized. Nevertheless, the Federal government was authorized to interfere in the internal affairs of the States *j in a few predetermined cases, in which a reckless abuse of their independence might endanger the security of the Union as a whole. Thus all the republics kept the power to modify and change their legislation at will, but they were forbidden to pass ex post facto laws or to create a class of nobles in their communities. *k Finally, since the Federal government had to be able to meet its obligations, it was given an unlimited power to levy taxes. *l
h [ See Constitution, sect. 8; “Federalist,” Nos. 41 and 42; Kent’s “Commentaries,” vol. i. p. 207; Story, pp. 358-382; Ibid. pp. 409-426.]

i [ Several other privileges of the same kind exist, such as the one that empowers the Union to legislate on bankruptcy, to grant patents, and to act in other matters where its intervention is clearly necessary.]
j [ Even in these cases its interference is indirect. The Union interferes by means of the tribunals, as will be shown later.]
k [ Federal Constitution, sect. 10, art. I.]
l [ Constitution, sects. 8, 9, and 10; “Federalist,” Nos. 30-36, inclusive, and 41-44; Kent’s “Commentaries,” vol. i. pp. 207 and 381; Story, pp. 329 and 514.]

Look at the balance of power the Federal Constitution established. On one side is the portion of sovereignty reserved to the several States; on the other is the share of power the Union has taken. It is plain that the Federal legislators had the clearest and most accurate ideas about the nature of centralization of government. The United States form not only a republic but a confederation. Nevertheless, the authority of the nation was more centralized than it was in several European monarchies when the American Constitution was framed. Take, for instance, the following two examples.

France had thirteen supreme courts of justice, which, generally speaking, had the right to interpret the law without appeal. The provinces called pays d’états were authorized to refuse their assent to a tax levied by the sovereign who represented the nation. In the Union there is only one tribunal to interpret the laws, just as there is only one legislature to make them, and a tax voted by the representatives of the nation binds all the citizens. On these two essential points, therefore, the Union exercises more central authority than the French monarchy possessed, although the Union is only an assemblage of confederate republics.

In Spain, certain provinces had the right to set up a system of customs duties of their own, although by its very nature that privilege belongs to national sovereignty. In America, Congress alone has the right to regulate the commercial relations of the States. In this respect, then, the government of the Confederation is more centralized than the kingdom of Spain. It is true that the power of the Crown in France or in Spain could always obtain by force whatever the country’s constitution denied it, and that the final result was therefore the same. But here I am discussing the theory of the Constitution.
Once the limits within which the Federal government was to act had been settled, the next point was to determine what powers it was to exercise.
Legislative Powers *m
m [ [In this chapter the author points out the essence of the conflict between the seceding States and the Union which caused the Civil War of 1861.]]

Division of the legislative body into two branches — Difference in the way the two Houses are formed — The principle of the independence of the States prevails in forming the Senate — The principle of the sovereignty of the nation prevails in composing the House of Representatives — Odd effects of the fact that a constitution can be logical only in the early stages of a nation.

The plan laid down earlier for the Constitutions of the several States was followed, on many points, in organizing the powers of the Union. The Federal legislature of the Union was composed of a Senate and a House of Representatives. A spirit of conciliation required that different principles be followed in forming these two assemblies. I have already shown that two opposed interests clashed when the Federal Constitution was established. These two interests had given rise to two opinions. One party wished to turn the Union into a league of independent States, or a kind of congress where the representatives of the several peoples would meet to discuss certain points of common interest. The other party wished to unite the inhabitants of the American colonies into a single nation and to set up a government that would act as the sole representative of the nation, as far as the limited sphere of its authority allowed. The practical consequences of these two theories were very different.

The question was whether a league was to be established in place of a national government, and whether the majority of the States, rather than the majority of the inhabitants of the Union, was to make the law. In that case every State, small or great, would keep the full enjoyment of its independence and would enter the Union on a footing of perfect equality. If, however, the inhabitants of the United States were to be regarded as belonging to one and the same nation, it would be just for the majority of the citizens of the Union to prescribe the law. Of course the smaller States could not accept this doctrine without in fact giving up their existence in relation to the sovereignty of the Confederation, since they would have gone from being a co-equal and co-legislative authority to being an insignificant fraction of a great people. If the first system would have given them excessive authority, the second would have wiped out their influence altogether. In these circumstances the strict rules of logic were evaded, as usually happens when interests are opposed to arguments. The legislators found a middle course, which forced together two systems that in theory could not be reconciled.

The principle of the independence of the States prevailed in forming the Senate, and the principle of the sovereignty of the nation prevailed in composing the House of Representatives. It was decided that each State should send two senators to Congress, and a number of representatives in proportion to its population. *n The result of this arrangement is that the State of New York today has forty representatives and only two senators, while the State of Delaware has two senators and only one representative. Delaware is therefore equal to New York in the Senate, while New York has forty times Delaware’s influence in the House of Representatives. Thus, if a minority of the nation prevails in the Senate, it may paralyze the decisions of the majority represented in the other House, which is contrary to the spirit of constitutional government.

n [ Every ten years Congress fixes anew the number of representatives each State is to send. The total number was 69 in 1789, and 240 in 1833. (See “American Almanac,” 1834, p. 194.) The Constitution decided that there should not be more than one representative for every 30,000 persons, but it set no minimum. Congress has not thought fit to increase the number of representatives in proportion to the growth of population. The first Act passed on the subject (April 14, 1792: see “Laws of the United States,” by Story, vol. i. p. 235) decided that there should be one representative for every 33,000 inhabitants. The last Act, passed in 1832, fixes the proportion at one for 48,000. The population represented is made up of all the free men and of three-fifths of the slaves.

[The last Act of apportionment, passed February 2, 1872, fixes the representation at one to 134,684 inhabitants. There are now (1875) 283 members of the lower House of Congress, and 9 for the States at large, making in all 292 members. The old States have of course lost the representatives which the new States have gained.—Translator’s Note.]]

These facts show how rare and how difficult it is to combine all the parts of a legislative system in a rational and logical way. In the course of time, different interests arise and the same people approves different principles. When a general constitution has to be established, these interests and principles are so many natural obstacles to the rigorous application of any political system with all its consequences. Only in the early stages of national existence is it possible to keep the logic of legislation complete. When we see a nation enjoying this advantage, we should remember, before we hurry to conclude that it is wise, that it is young. When the Federal Constitution was formed, the interest of independence for the separate States and the interest of union for the whole people were the only two conflicting interests among the Anglo-Americans, and a compromise between them was inevitable.

It is only fair to acknowledge, however, that so far this part of the Constitution has not produced the evils that might have been feared. All the States are young and neighboring; their customs, their ideas, and their needs are not dissimilar; and the differences that come from their size or smallness are not enough to set their interests at odds. The small States have therefore never been led to band together in the Senate against the designs of the larger ones. Indeed, the legitimate expression of the will of a people carries such irresistible authority that the Senate could offer only feeble opposition to the vote of the majority of the House of Representatives.

It must not be forgotten, on the other hand, that it was not in the power of the American legislators to reduce to a single nation the people for whom they were making laws. The object of the Federal Constitution was not to destroy the independence of the States but to restrain it. By acknowledging the real authority of these secondary communities (and it was impossible to deprive them of it), the legislators disavowed in advance any habitual use of force to carry out the decisions of the majority. On this principle there was nothing surprising in bringing the influence of the States into the machinery of the Federal government. It merely attested the existence of a recognized power, which had to be handled with tact and not forcibly checked.
A Further Difference Between the Senate and the House of Representatives

The Senate is named by the legislatures of the States, the Representatives by the people — The former are elected twice over, the latter once — Term of the different offices — The particular functions of each House.

The Senate differs from the other House not only in the principle it represents but also in the way it is elected, in the term for which it is chosen, and in the nature of its functions. The House of Representatives is named by the people, the Senate by the legislators of each State. The former is elected directly, the latter by an elected body. Representatives are chosen for only two years, senators for six. The functions of the House of Representatives are purely legislative, and its only share in the judicial power is the impeachment of public officials. The Senate cooperates in the work of legislation, and it tries those political offenses that the House of Representatives submits to its decision. It also acts as the great executive council of the nation. Treaties concluded by the President must be ratified by the Senate, and the appointments he makes must be finally approved by the same body. *o
o [ See “The Federalist,” Nos. 52-56, inclusive; Story, pp. 199-314; Constitution of the United States, sects. 2 and 3.] The Executive Power *p
p [ See “The Federalist,” Nos. 67-77; Constitution of the United States, art. 2; Story, p. 315, pp. 615-780; Kent’s “Commentaries,” p. 255.]

Dependence of the President — He is elected and answerable — He is free to act in his own sphere under the inspection, but not the direction, of the Senate — His salary is fixed when he enters office — Suspensive veto.

The American legislators took on a difficult task when they tried to create an executive power that would depend on the majority of the people and yet be strong enough to act without restraint in its own sphere. To preserve the republican form of government, it was essential that the representative of the executive power be subject to the will of the nation.

The President is an elected magistrate. His honor, his property, his liberty, and his life are the guarantees the people holds that he will use his power with moderation. But in exercising his authority he cannot be called perfectly independent. The Senate takes notice of his relations with foreign powers and of how he distributes public appointments, so that he can neither be bribed nor use the means of corruption himself. The legislators of the Union recognized that the executive power could not carry out its task with dignity and usefulness unless it had greater stability and strength than it had been given in the separate States.

The President is chosen for four years and may be reelected. The prospect of a long administration may thus inspire him with hopeful undertakings for the public good, and give him the means of carrying them out. The President was made the sole representative of the executive power of the Union, and care was taken not to make his decisions subject to the vote of a council. That would have been a dangerous measure, which tends both to clog the action of the government and to reduce its responsibility. The Senate has the right to annul certain acts of the President, but it cannot compel him to take any step, nor does it share in the exercise of the executive power.

The legislature’s action on the executive power may be direct, and we have just shown that the Americans carefully prevented this influence. But it may also be indirect. Public assemblies that have the power to deprive an officer of state of his salary encroach on his independence. And since they are free to make the laws, there is reason to fear that they may gradually take for themselves a portion of the authority the Constitution placed in his hands. This dependence of the executive power is one of the defects inherent in republican constitutions. The Americans have not been able to counteract the tendency of legislative assemblies to take possession of the government, but they have made this tendency less irresistible. The President’s salary is fixed, when he enters office, for the whole period of his magistracy. The President is also given a suspensive veto, which allows him to oppose the passing of laws that might destroy the portion of independence the Constitution grants him. The struggle between the President and the legislature must always be an unequal one, since the legislature is certain to overcome all resistance if it persists in its plans. But the suspensive veto at least forces it to reconsider the matter, and if it persists in the motion, the motion must then be backed by a majority of two-thirds of the whole house. The veto is, in fact, a kind of appeal to the people. Without this security, the executive power might have been oppressed in secret. By the veto it pleads its cause and states its reasons. Suppose someone objects that the legislature is certain to overcome all resistance by persisting in its plans. I reply that in the constitutions of all nations, of whatever kind, there is a certain point at which the legislator must rely on the good sense and the virtue of his fellow citizens. This point is more prominent and easier to find in republics, and more remote and more carefully hidden in monarchies, but it always exists somewhere. There is no country in the world where everything can be provided for by the laws, or where political institutions can take the place of common sense and public morality.
Differences Between the Position of the President of the United States and That of a Constitutional King of France

Executive power in the Northern States is as limited and partial as the supremacy it represents — Executive power in France is as universal as the supremacy it represents — The King is a branch of the legislature — The President is the mere executor of the law — Other differences arising from the duration of the two powers — The President is checked in exercising executive authority — The King is independent in exercising it — Despite these differences, France is more akin to a republic than the Union is to a monarchy — Comparison of the number of public officials who depend on the executive power in the two countries.

The executive power has so important an influence on the destinies of nations that I am inclined to pause for a moment on this part of my subject, in order to explain more clearly the part it plays in America. To form an accurate idea of the position of the President of the United States, it may be useful to compare it with that of one of the constitutional kings of Europe. In this comparison I shall pay little attention to the outward signs of power, which are more apt to mislead the observer than to guide his inquiry. When a monarchy is gradually transformed into a republic, the executive power keeps the titles, the honors, the etiquette, and even the funds of royalty long after its authority has disappeared. The English cut off the head of one king and drove another from his throne, and yet they were used to approaching the successor of those princes on their knees. On the other hand, when a republic falls under the sway of a single individual, the sovereign’s bearing is simple and unpretending, as if his authority were not yet supreme. When the emperors had unlimited control over the fortunes and the lives of their fellow citizens, it was customary to call them Caesar in conversation, and they were in the habit of dining informally at their friends’ houses. It is therefore necessary to look beneath the surface.

Sovereignty in the United States is shared between the Union and the States, while in France it is undivided and compact. From this arises the first and most notable difference between the President of the United States and the King of France. In the United States the executive power is as limited and partial as the sovereignty of the Union in whose name it acts. In France it is as universal as the authority of the state. The Americans have a federal government and the French a national government.

This cause of inferiority results from the nature of things, but it is not the only one. The second in importance is as follows. Sovereignty may be defined as the right to make laws. In France the King really exercises a portion of the sovereign power, since the laws have no force until he has given his assent to them. He is, moreover, the executor of everything they ordain. The President is also the executor of the laws, but he does not really take part in making them, since his refusal of assent does not annul them. He is therefore to be considered merely as the agent of the sovereign power. But the King of France not only exercises a portion of the sovereign power; he also helps to name the legislature, which exercises the other portion. He has the privilege of appointing the members of one chamber and of dissolving the other at his pleasure. The President of the United States has no share in forming the legislative body and cannot dissolve any part of it. The King has the same right as the Chambers to bring forward measures, a right the President does not have. The King is represented in each assembly by his ministers, who explain his intentions, support his opinions, and defend the principles of the government. The President and his ministers are alike excluded from Congress, so that his influence and his opinions can reach that great body only indirectly. The King of France therefore stands on an equal footing with the legislature, which can no more act without him than he can without it. The President exercises an authority that is inferior to that of the legislature and depends on it.

Even in exercising the executive power properly so called, the point on which his position seems most like that of the King of France, the President labors under several causes of inferiority. First, the authority of the King in France has the advantage of duration over that of the President, and durability is one of the chief elements of strength. People love or fear only what is likely to last. The President of the United States is a magistrate elected for four years; the King of France is a hereditary sovereign. In exercising the executive power, the President of the United States is constantly under jealous scrutiny. He may negotiate a treaty but cannot conclude it; he may nominate a public official but cannot appoint him. *q The King of France is absolute within the limits of his authority. The President of the United States is answerable for his actions, but the person of the King is declared inviolable by the French Charter. *r

q [ The Constitution had left it doubtful whether the President was obliged to consult the Senate in removing as well as in appointing Federal officers. “The Federalist” (No. 77) seemed to establish that he was. But in 1789 Congress formally decided that, since the President was responsible for his actions, he ought not to be forced to employ agents who had lost his esteem. See Kent’s “Commentaries”, vol. i. p. 289.]
r [ [This comparison applied to the Constitutional King of France and to the powers he held under the Charter of 1830, till the overthrow of the monarchy in 1848.—Translator’s Note.]]

Nevertheless, the supremacy of public opinion stands over the head of the one no less than over the other. This power is less definite, less evident, and less backed by the laws in France than in America, but in fact it exists. In America it acts through elections and decrees; in France it proceeds by revolutions. But despite the different constitutions of the two countries, public opinion is the dominant authority in both. The fundamental principle of legislation, a principle essentially republican, is the same in both countries, although its consequences may differ and its results may be more or less far-reaching. From this I am led to conclude that France with its King is nearer to being a republic than the Union with its President is to being a monarchy.

In what I have been saying I have touched only on the main points of difference. If I could have gone into details, the contrast would have been even more striking. I have observed that the authority of the President in the United States is exercised only within the limits of a partial sovereignty, while that of the King in France is undivided. I could go on to show that the power of the King’s government in France goes beyond its natural limits, wide as they are, and reaches in a thousand different ways into the management of private interests. One example of this influence is the great number of public officials, all of whom owe their appointments to the government. This number now exceeds all previous limits; it comes to 138,000 *s nominations, each of which may be regarded as an element of power. The President of the United States has no exclusive right to make any public appointments, and their whole number scarcely exceeds 12,000. *t
s [ The sums annually paid by the State to these officers amount to 200,000,000 fr. ($40,000,000).]

t [ This number is extracted from the “National Calendar” for 1833. The “National Calendar” is an American almanac that contains the names of all the Federal officers. The comparison shows that the King of France has eleven times as many places at his disposal as the President, although the population of France is not much more than double that of the Union.

[I have no means of finding out the number of appointments now at the disposal of the President of the United States, but his patronage and the abuse of it have greatly increased since 1833.—Translator’s Note, 1875.]]
Accidental Causes That May Increase the Influence of the Executive Government
External security of the Union — An army of six thousand men — Few ships — The President has no opportunity to exercise his great prerogatives — In the prerogatives he does exercise he is weak.
If the executive government is weaker in America than in France, the cause lies more in circumstances than in the laws of the country.

It is chiefly in its foreign relations that the executive power of a nation is called on to show its skill and its vigor. If the existence of the Union were constantly threatened, and if its chief interests were in daily contact with those of other powerful nations, the executive government would grow in importance in proportion to what was expected of it and to what it carried out. The President of the United States is commander-in-chief of the army, but of an army of only six thousand men. He commands the fleet, but the fleet has only a few ships. He conducts the foreign relations of the Union, but the United States is a nation without neighbors. Separated from the rest of the world by the ocean, and still too weak to aim at dominion over the seas, the United States has no enemies, and its interests rarely come into contact with those of any other nation on the globe.

The practical working of a government must not be judged by the theory of its constitution. The President of the United States possesses almost royal prerogatives, which he has no opportunity to exercise. The privileges he can use at present are very limited. The laws allow him a degree of influence that circumstances do not let him employ.

On the other hand, the great strength of the royal prerogative in France comes far more from circumstances than from the laws. There the executive government is constantly struggling against enormous obstacles and straining all its energies to overcome them. It therefore grows with the extent of its achievements and the importance of the events it controls, without any change in its constitution. If the laws had made it as weak and as limited as it is in the Union, its influence would very soon become still more dominant.

Why the President of the United States Does Not Require the Majority of the Two Houses in Order to Carry On the Government It is an established axiom in Europe that a constitutional king cannot persevere in a system of government opposed by the other two branches of the legislature. Yet several Presidents of the United States have lost the majority in the legislative body without having to give up supreme power and without doing serious harm to society. I have heard this fact cited as proof of the independence and strength of the executive government in America. A moment’s reflection will convince us that it proves the opposite: the executive’s extreme weakness.

A king in Europe needs the support of the legislature to carry out the duties the Constitution gives him, because those duties are enormous. A constitutional king in Europe does not merely execute the law. Carrying out its provisions depends so completely on him that he can paralyze its effect if it runs against his plans. He needs the legislative assemblies to make the law, but those assemblies need his help to carry it out. Neither authority can survive without the other, and the machinery of government stops as soon as they are at odds.

In America the President cannot prevent any law from being passed, and he cannot escape the obligation to enforce it. His sincere and zealous cooperation is no doubt useful, but it is not indispensable to the conduct of public affairs. All his important acts are submitted, directly or indirectly, to the legislature, and on his own authority he can do very little. It is therefore his weakness, and not his power, that allows him to remain in opposition to Congress. In Europe, harmony must prevail between the Crown and the other branches of the legislature, because a collision between them could prove serious. In America this harmony is not indispensable, because such a collision is impossible.
Election of the President

Dangers of the elective system increase in proportion to the extent of the prerogative — This system is possible in America because no powerful executive authority is required — What circumstances are favorable to the elective system — Why the election of the President does not cause a departure from the principles of the government — Influence of the election of the President on secondary officials.

Experience and history have sufficiently shown the dangers of electing the head of the executive government of a great people, and the remarks I am about to make concern America alone. These dangers may be more or less formidable depending on the place the executive power occupies in the State and the importance it has there. They may also vary according to the mode of election and the circumstances of the electors. The weightiest argument against electing a chief magistrate is that the office offers so splendid a lure to private ambition, and so easily inflames men in the pursuit of power, that when legitimate means fail, force may often seize what right denied.

Clearly, the greater the privileges of the executive authority, the greater the temptation. The more the candidates’ ambition is excited, the more warmly their interests are taken up by a throng of partisans who hope to share the power once their patron has won the prize. The dangers of the elective system therefore increase in exact proportion to the influence the executive power exercises in the affairs of State. The revolutions of Poland were not due to the elective system alone, but to the fact that the elected monarch was the sovereign of a powerful kingdom. Before we can discuss the absolute advantages of the elective system, we must first ask whether the geographical position, the laws, the habits, the customs, and the opinions of the people among whom it is to be introduced will allow a weak and dependent executive government to be established. For in my opinion, to try to make the representative of the State both a powerful sovereign and an elected one is to pursue two incompatible aims. I know of only one way to reduce hereditary royalty to the condition of an elective authority: first confine its sphere of action, then gradually reduce its prerogatives, and accustom the people to live without its protection. Yet nothing is further from the intentions of the republicans of Europe than this course. Many of them owe their hatred of tyranny to the sufferings they have personally undergone, so it is oppression, and not the extent of the executive power, that provokes their hostility. They attack the one without seeing how closely it is connected with the other.

So far, no citizen has shown any willingness to risk his honor and his life in order to become President of the United States, because the power of that office is temporary, limited, and subordinate. The prize of fortune would have to be great to tempt adventurers into so desperate a game. No candidate has yet been able to arouse dangerous enthusiasm or passionate sympathy among the people in his favor, for the very simple reason that once he is at the head of the government he has little power, little wealth, and little glory to share among his friends. His influence in the State is too small for the success or ruin of a faction to depend on one individual’s rise to power.

The great advantage of hereditary monarchies is that a family’s private interest is always closely bound up with the interests of the State, so the executive government is never suspended for a single instant. If the affairs of a monarchy are not better managed than those of a republic, at least there is always someone to manage them, well or badly, according to his ability. In elective States, by contrast, the wheels of government seem to stop of their own accord as an election approaches, and even for some time before it. The laws can indeed speed up the election, which may be conducted so simply and quickly that the seat of power is never left vacant. Despite these precautions, however, a break inevitably occurs in the minds of the people.

As an election approaches, the head of the executive government is wholly taken up with the coming struggle. His future plans are uncertain, he can undertake nothing new, and he will pursue only with indifference designs that another man may have to finish. “I am so near the time of my retirement from office,” said President Jefferson on the 21st of January, 1809 (six weeks before the election), “that I feel no passion, I take no part, I express no sentiment. It appears to me just to leave to my successor the commencement of those measures which he will have to prosecute, and for which he will be responsible.”

On the other hand, the eyes of the nation are fixed on a single point, and everyone is watching the gradual approach of so important an event. The wider the influence of the executive power, the greater and more necessary its constant action, and the more fatal this period of suspense becomes. A nation accustomed to such a government, and still more one used to the administrative protection of a powerful executive authority, would inevitably be convulsed by an election of this kind. In the United States the action of the government can be slackened with impunity, because it is always weak and narrowly limited. *u

u [ [This, however, may be a great danger. The period during which Mr. Buchanan held office after the election of Mr. Lincoln, from November 1860 to March 1861, was the one that allowed the seceding States of the South to complete their preparations for the Civil War, while the executive government was paralyzed. No greater evil could befall a nation.—Translator’s Note.]]

One of the principal vices of the elective system is that it always introduces a certain degree of instability into the internal and foreign policy of the State. But this disadvantage is felt less when the elected magistrate holds only a small share of power. In Rome the principles of government underwent no change, although the Consuls were replaced every year, because the Senate, a hereditary assembly, held the directing authority. If the elective system were adopted in Europe, the condition of most monarchical States would change with every new election. In America the President has a certain influence on affairs of State, but he does not conduct them. The preponderant power lies with the representatives of the whole nation. The country’s political maxims therefore depend on the mass of the people and not on the President alone, and so in America the elective system has no very harmful effect on the fixed principles of the government. But the lack of fixed principles is an evil so inherent in the elective system that it is still very noticeable even within the narrow sphere of the President’s authority.

The Americans have accepted that the head of the executive power, who bears the whole responsibility for the duties he is called on to fulfill, ought to be empowered to choose his own agents and to remove them at will. The legislative bodies watch the President’s conduct more than they direct it. The consequence is that with every new election the fate of all the Federal public officers hangs in the balance. Mr. Quincy Adams, on taking office, dismissed most of the people his predecessor had appointed. And I do not know of a single removable official in the Federal service whom General Jackson allowed to keep his place beyond the first year after his election. People sometimes complain that in the constitutional monarchies of Europe the fate of the humbler servants of an administration depends on that of the ministers. But in elective governments this evil is far greater. In a constitutional monarchy, successive ministries are formed quickly. Because the principal representative of the executive power does not change, however, the spirit of innovation is kept within bounds, and the changes that occur affect the details of the administrative system rather than its principles. But to replace one system with another, as is done in America every four years by law, is to cause a kind of revolution. As for the hardships this may bring on individuals, it must be admitted that the uncertain position of public officers has fewer harmful consequences in America than elsewhere. It is so easy to gain an independent position in the United States that a public officer who loses his place may be deprived of the comforts of life, but not of the means of subsistence.

I noted at the beginning of this chapter that the dangers of electing the head of the State are increased or reduced by the particular circumstances of the people that adopts the system. However restricted the functions of the executive power may be, it must always have great influence on the country’s foreign policy, because a negotiation cannot be opened or carried on successfully except through a single agent. The more precarious and perilous a people’s position becomes, the more absolutely it needs a fixed and consistent foreign policy, and the more dangerous the election of the Chief Magistrate becomes. The policy of the Americans toward the rest of the world is extremely simple. It may almost be said that no country needs them, and they do not need the cooperation of any other people. Their independence is never threatened. In their present condition, therefore, the functions of the executive power are limited by circumstances no less than by the laws, and the President can often change his line of policy without bringing difficulty or ruin on the State.

Whatever the prerogatives of the executive power, the period just before an election and the time it lasts must always be considered a national crisis, and its peril is proportional to the country’s internal difficulties and external dangers. Few of the nations of Europe could escape the calamities of anarchy or conquest every time they had to elect a new sovereign. In America society is so constituted that it can stand on its own foundation without assistance. Nothing is to be feared from the pressure of external dangers, and the election of the President is a cause of agitation but not of ruin.

Skill of the American legislators shown in the mode of election they adopted — Creation of a special electoral body — Separate votes of these electors — Case in which the House of Representatives is called on to choose the President — Results of the twelve elections that have taken place since the Constitution was established.

Besides the dangers inherent in the system itself, many other difficulties may arise from the mode of election, and the legislator’s foresight can prevent them. When a people gathered under arms in some public place to choose its head, it faced all the risks of civil war that so martial a procedure brought, in addition to the dangers of the elective system itself. The Polish laws, which made the election of the sovereign subject to the veto of a single individual, invited the murder of that individual or prepared the way for anarchy.

In examining the institutions and the political and social condition of the United States, we are struck by the admirable harmony between the gifts of fortune and the efforts of man. The nation possessed two of the main causes of internal peace: it was a new country, but it was inhabited by a people grown old in the exercise of freedom. America had no hostile neighbors to fear. Taking advantage of these favorable circumstances, the American legislators created a weak and subordinate executive power that could be made elective without danger.

It then remained only for them to choose the least dangerous of the various modes of election. The rules they laid down on this point correspond admirably to the safeguards the country’s physical and political constitution already provided. Their aim was to find the mode of election that would best express the people’s choice with the least possible excitement and suspense. First, it was agreed that a simple majority should decide, but the difficulty was to obtain this majority without the delay that it was most important to avoid. It rarely happens that one individual can immediately gather the majority of the votes of a great people. The difficulty is greater still in a republic of confederate States, where local influences tend to predominate. The means proposed to overcome this second obstacle was to delegate the nation’s electoral powers to a body of representatives. This mode of election made a majority more probable, for the fewer the electors, the greater the chance that they will reach a final decision. It also offered an added likelihood of a wise choice. It then remained to decide whether to entrust this right of election to a legislative body, the nation’s ordinary representative assembly, or to form an electoral assembly for the express purpose of nominating a President. The Americans chose the latter alternative. They believed that the individuals elected to make the laws were not fit to represent the nation’s wishes in electing its chief magistrate, and that, since they are chosen for more than a year, the constituency they represent might change its opinion in that time. They thought that if the legislature were empowered to elect the head of the executive power, its members would be exposed, for some time before the election, to the maneuvers of corruption and the tricks of intrigue. The special electors, by contrast, would remain mixed in with the crowd, like a jury, until the day of action, when they would appear for the sole purpose of casting their votes.

It was therefore established that every State should name a certain number of electors, *v who in turn should elect the President. It had been observed that in elective countries the assemblies entrusted with choosing a chief magistrate inevitably became centers of passion and cabal. It had also been observed that they sometimes seized an authority that did not belong to them, and that their proceedings, or the uncertainty these produced, were sometimes prolonged so far as to endanger the welfare of the State. It was therefore decided that the electors should all vote on the same day without being convened in the same place. *w This double election made a majority probable, though not certain, for as many differences might exist among the electors as among their constituents. In that case one of three measures had to be used: appoint new electors, consult the existing electors a second time, or hand the election to another authority. The first two alternatives, apart from the uncertainty of their results, were likely to delay the final decision and to prolong an agitation that is always dangerous. The third expedient was therefore adopted. It was agreed that the votes should be sent sealed to the President of the Senate and opened and counted in the presence of the Senate and the House of Representatives. If no candidate has a majority, the House of Representatives immediately proceeds to elect a President, on the condition that it must choose from the three candidates with the highest numbers. *x
v [ As many as it sends members to Congress. The number of electors at the election of 1833 was 288. (See “The National Calendar,” 1833.)]

w [ The electors of the same State assemble, but they transmit to the central government the list of their individual votes, and not the mere result of the vote of the majority.] [Footnote x: In this case it is the majority of the States, and not the majority of the members, that decides the question, so that New York has no more influence in the debate than Rhode Island. Thus the citizens of the Union are first consulted as members of one and the same community. If they cannot agree, recourse is had to a division by States, each of which has a separate and independent vote. This is one of the oddities of the Federal Constitution, and it can be explained only by the clash of conflicting interests.]

Thus the election is entrusted to the ordinary representatives of the nation only in the event of something that cannot happen often and can never be foreseen. Even then they must choose a citizen already designated by a powerful minority of the special electors. This happy expedient combines respect for the voice of the people with the greatest speed of execution and with the precautions the peace of the country demands. But the House of Representatives’ decision does not necessarily settle the difficulty at once, for the majority of that assembly may still be undecided, and in that case the Constitution prescribes no remedy. Nevertheless, by limiting the candidates to three and by referring the matter to the judgment of an enlightened public body, it has removed all the obstacles *y that are not inherent in the elective system.
y [ Jefferson, in 1801, was not elected until the thirty-sixth time of balloting.]

In the forty-four years since the Federal Constitution was promulgated, the United States has chosen a President twelve times. Ten of these elections took place simultaneously, by the votes of the special electors in the different States. The House of Representatives has used its conditional privilege of deciding uncertain cases only twice: the first time was at the election of Mr. Jefferson in 1801, and the second was in 1825, when Mr. Quincy Adams was named. *z
z [ [General Grant is now (1874) the eighteenth President of the United States.]]
Crises of the Election
The election may be considered a national crisis — Why? — Passions of the people — Anxiety of the President — Calm that follows the agitation of the election.

I have shown what circumstances favored the adoption of the elective system in the United States, and what precautions the legislators took to guard against its dangers. The Americans are accustomed to every kind of election, and they know from experience the highest degree of excitement that is compatible with safety. The vast extent of the country and the scattering of its inhabitants make a collision between parties less likely and less dangerous there than elsewhere. The political circumstances in which elections have been conducted so far have caused the nation no real difficulty.

Nevertheless, the time of a presidential election in the United States may be considered a crisis in the affairs of the nation. The President’s influence on public business is no doubt weak and indirect. But the choice of President, which matters little to each individual citizen, concerns the citizens collectively, and however trifling an interest may be, it becomes very important as soon as it becomes general. Compared with the kings of Europe, the President has few means of rewarding his supporters. But the offices at his disposal are numerous enough to interest several thousand electors, directly or indirectly, in his success. Political parties in the United States are led to rally around an individual in order to take a more tangible shape in the eyes of the crowd, and the name of the candidate for the Presidency is held up as the symbol and personification of their theories. For these reasons parties have a strong interest in winning the election. They want less to see their principles triumph under the President-elect than to show, by the majority that elected him, how strong the supporters of those principles are.

For a long time before the appointed day, the election becomes the most important topic of discussion and absorbs everyone’s attention. The ardor of faction redoubles, and every artificial passion that the imagination can create in the heart of a happy and peaceful land is stirred up and brought to light. The President, for his part, is absorbed in the cares of self-defense. He no longer governs in the interest of the State, but in the interest of his reelection. He pays homage to the majority, and instead of checking its passions as his duty requires, he often courts its worst whims. As the election draws near, intrigue grows more active and the populace more agitated. The citizens divide into hostile camps, each taking the name of its favorite candidate. The whole nation glows with feverish excitement. The election is the daily theme of the public papers, the subject of private conversation, the goal of every thought and every action, the sole interest of the present. As soon as the choice is made, this ardor dies away. A calmer season returns, and the current of the State, which had nearly broken its banks, sinks back to its usual level. *a But who can help being astonished at the causes of the storm?

Reelection of the President

When the head of the executive power can be reelected, it is the State that becomes the source of intrigue and corruption — The desire to be reelected is the chief aim of a President of the United States — A disadvantage of the system peculiar to America — The natural evil of democracy is that it subordinates all authority to the slightest desires of the majority — The reelection of the President encourages this evil.

It may be asked whether the legislators of the United States were right or wrong to allow the reelection of the President. At first sight it seems contrary to all reason to prevent the head of the executive power from being elected a second time. The influence that one individual’s talents and character may have on the fate of a whole people, in critical circumstances or difficult times, is well known. A law preventing the reelection of the chief magistrate would deprive the citizens of the surest pledge of the commonwealth’s prosperity and security. And, by a strange inconsistency, a man would be excluded from the government at the very moment he had shown his ability to conduct its affairs.

But if these arguments are strong, perhaps still more powerful reasons can be put forward against them. Intrigue and corruption are the natural vices of elective government. When the head of the State can be reelected, however, these evils rise to a great height and endanger the very existence of the country. When a simple candidate seeks to rise by intrigue, his maneuvers are necessarily confined to a narrow sphere. When the chief magistrate enters the contest, he borrows the strength of the government for his own purposes. In the first case, the feeble resources of one individual are at work. In the second, the State itself, with all its immense influence, is busy with corruption and cabal. A private citizen who uses the most immoral practices to gain power can harm the public prosperity only indirectly. But if the representative of the executive descends into the fight, the cares of government shrink to second-rate importance, and winning his election becomes his first concern. All the laws and all the negotiations he undertakes are to him nothing more than electioneering schemes. Offices become the reward of services rendered not to the nation but to its chief. And the influence of the government, if not harmful to the country, is at least no longer beneficial to the community for which it was created.

It is impossible to look at the ordinary course of affairs in the United States without seeing that the desire to be reelected is the President’s chief aim. His whole administration, even his most indifferent measures, tends toward this object. As the crisis approaches, his personal interest takes the place of his interest in the public good. The principle of reeligibility makes the corrupting influence of elective government still more extensive and harmful.

In America this principle has a particularly fatal effect on the sources of national life. Every government seems to suffer from some evil inherent in its nature, and the legislator’s genius is shown in avoiding its attacks. A State may survive the influence of a host of bad laws, and the harm they cause is often exaggerated. But a law that encourages the growth of the canker within must prove fatal in the end, even if its bad consequences are not immediately seen.

The principle of destruction in absolute monarchies lies in the excessive and unreasonable extension of the crown’s prerogative. A measure that removed the constitutional provisions counterbalancing this influence would be radically bad, even if its immediate consequences did no harm. By the same reasoning, in countries governed by a democracy, where the people is constantly drawing all authority to itself, laws that increase or speed up its action are direct assaults on the very principle of the government.

The greatest proof of the American legislators’ ability is that they saw this truth clearly and had the courage to act on it. They held that there had to be a certain authority above the body of the people. It would enjoy a degree of independence without being entirely beyond popular control. It would be forced to comply with the majority’s lasting decisions, but would be able to resist its whims and refuse its most dangerous demands. To this end they concentrated the whole executive power of the nation in a single hand. They granted the President extensive prerogatives, and they armed him with the veto to resist the encroachments of the legislature.

But by introducing the principle of reelection, they partly undid their own work. They made the President little inclined to use the great power they had placed in his hands. If he could not be elected a second time, the President would be far from independent of the people, for his responsibility would not be lessened. But the people’s favor would not be so necessary to him that he would court it by humoring its desires. If he can be reelected (and this is especially true today, when political morality is relaxed and great men are rare), the President of the United States becomes an easy tool in the hands of the majority. He adopts its likes and its dislikes. He hurries to anticipate its wishes and forestall its complaints, and he yields to its idlest cravings. Instead of guiding it, as the legislature intended, he is always ready to follow its orders. Thus, in order not to deprive the State of one individual’s talents, those talents have been made almost useless. And in order to keep an expedient in reserve for extraordinary dangers, the country has been exposed to daily dangers.

I have examined the legislative and executive power of the Union, and the judicial power remains to be studied. But here I cannot hide my fears from the reader. The judicial institutions of the Anglo-Americans have great influence on their condition, and they hold a prominent place among what are properly called political institutions. In this respect they deserve our special attention. But I find it hard to explain the political role of the American tribunals without going into some technical details of their constitution and their forms of procedure. And I do not know how to descend to these minutiae without wearying the reader’s curiosity with the natural dryness of the subject, or without risking obscurity in my effort to be brief. I can hardly hope to escape these various evils. If I seem too long to a man of the world, a lawyer may complain of my brevity. But these are the natural drawbacks of my subject, and especially of the point I am about to discuss.

The great difficulty was not to design a Constitution for the Federal government, but to find a way of enforcing its laws. Governments generally have only two means of overcoming the opposition of the people they govern: the physical force at their own disposal, and the moral force they draw from the decisions of the courts of justice.

A government with no other means of demanding obedience than open war would be very near its ruin, for one of two things would probably happen. If its authority was slight and its character moderate, it would not resort to violence until the last extremity. It would overlook a number of partial acts of insubordination, and the State would gradually fall into anarchy. If it was enterprising and powerful, it would constantly fall back on its physical strength and would quickly degenerate into a military despotism. Its activity would then be no less harmful to the community than its inaction.

The great end of justice is to substitute the idea of right for that of violence, and to place a legal barrier between the power of the government and the use of physical force. The authority that the general opinion of mankind grants to the intervention of a court of justice is so surprisingly great that it clings to the mere formalities of justice and gives physical weight to the shadow of the law. The moral force that courts of justice possess makes the use of physical force exceedingly rare, and very often takes its place. And if physical force proves indispensable, its power is doubled by the association with the idea of law.

A federal government needs the support of judicial institutions more than any other, because it is naturally weak and exposed to formidable opposition. *c If it were always obliged to resort to violence in the first instance, it could not fulfill its task. The Union therefore needed a national judiciary to enforce the citizens’ obedience to the laws and to repel attacks that might be directed against them. The question then was which tribunals should exercise these powers. Should they be entrusted to the courts of justice already organized in every State? Or was it necessary to create federal courts? It is easy to prove that the Union could not adapt the judicial power of the States to its needs. The separation of the judiciary from the administrative power of the State no doubt affects the security of every citizen and the liberty of all. But it is no less important to the life of the nation that these several powers should have the same origin, follow the same principles, and act in the same sphere. In a word, they should be correlative and homogeneous. No one, I presume, ever suggested the advantage of trying offenses committed in France before a foreign court of justice, in order to secure the judges’ impartiality. The Americans form one people in relation to their Federal government. But within this people various political bodies have been allowed to remain in existence. They depend on the national government in a few points and are independent in all the rest. Each has a distinct origin, maxims peculiar to itself, and its own means of carrying on its affairs. To entrust the execution of the laws of the Union to tribunals set up by these political bodies would be to allow foreign judges to preside over the nation. More than that, each State is not only foreign to the Union at large, but in perpetual opposition to the common interests, since whatever authority the Union loses turns to the advantage of the States. Thus to enforce the laws of the Union through the tribunals of the States would be to allow judges who are not only foreign but partial to preside over the nation.

c [ Federal laws are the ones that most need courts of justice, and at the same time the ones for which courts have most rarely been established. The reason is that confederations have usually been formed by independent States that had no real intention of obeying the central government, that very readily ceded the right of command to the federal executive, and that very prudently reserved the right of non-compliance for themselves.]

But the number of the State tribunals, even more than their character, made them unfit to serve the nation. When the Federal Constitution was formed, there were already thirteen courts of justice in the United States deciding cases without appeal. That number has now grown to twenty-four. To suppose that a State can survive when its fundamental laws may be subjected to twenty-four different interpretations at the same time is to advance a proposition contrary to both reason and experience.

The American legislators therefore agreed to create a federal judiciary to apply the laws of the Union and to decide certain questions affecting general interests, which were carefully defined in advance. The entire judicial power of the Union was concentrated in one tribunal, called the Supreme Court of the United States. But to speed the dispatch of business, inferior courts were attached to it. These were empowered to decide cases of small importance without appeal, and cases of greater magnitude with appeal. The members of the Supreme Court are named neither by the people nor by the legislature, but by the President of the United States, acting with the advice of the Senate. To make them independent of the other authorities, their office was made irremovable, and it was decided that once their salary was fixed, the legislature could not alter it. *d It was easy to proclaim the principle of a Federal judiciary, but difficulties multiplied when the extent of its jurisdiction had to be determined.

Means of Determining the Jurisdiction of the Federal Courts The difficulty of defining the jurisdiction of separate courts in confederations — The courts of the Union received the right to fix their own jurisdiction — In what way this rule infringes on the portion of sovereignty reserved to the several States — The sovereignty of these States is limited by the laws and by the interpretation of the laws — Hence the danger to the States is more apparent than real.

The Constitution of the United States recognized two distinct powers confronting each other, represented in the judicial sphere by two distinct classes of courts. Even the greatest care in defining their separate jurisdictions could not have prevented frequent collisions between those tribunals. The question then arose: who should have the right to decide the competence of each court?

In nations that form a single body politic, when two courts dispute their mutual jurisdiction, a third tribunal is generally at hand to settle the difference. This is done without difficulty, because in such nations questions of judicial competence have no bearing on the privileges of national supremacy. But it was impossible to create an arbiter between a superior court of the Union and the superior court of a separate State that would not itself belong to one of those two classes. It was therefore necessary to let one of the courts judge its own cause, and take or keep cognizance of the point in dispute. To grant this privilege to the courts of the States would have destroyed the sovereignty of the Union in fact after establishing it in law; for the interpretation of the Constitution would soon have given back to the States the very portion of independence that the terms of that act took from them. The purpose of creating a Federal tribunal was to stop the courts of the States from deciding, each in its own sphere, questions affecting national interests, and so to form a uniform body of jurisprudence for the interpretation of the laws of the Union. This purpose would not have been achieved if the courts of the several States had been competent to decide, in their separate capacities, cases from which they were obliged to abstain as Federal tribunals. The Supreme Court of the United States was therefore given the right to determine all questions of jurisdiction. *e

e [ To cut down on such suits, many Federal cases were made open to the courts of the States as well as those of the Union, and the party who loses has a right to appeal to the Supreme Court of the United States. The Supreme Court of Virginia denied that the Supreme Court of the United States could hear an appeal from its decisions, but it did not prevail. See “Kent’s Commentaries,” vol. i. p. 300, pp. 370 et seq.; Story’s “Commentaries,” p. 646; and “The Organic Law of the United States,” vol. i. p. 35.]

This was a heavy blow to the independence of the States. They were now bound not only by the laws but by the interpretation of the laws: by one limit that was known and another that was uncertain, by a rule that was fixed and another that was arbitrary. The Constitution did lay down the exact limits of Federal supremacy, yet whenever a State disputes that supremacy, a Federal tribunal rules on the question. Still, the threat this arrangement posed to the independence of the States is less serious than it looks. We shall see later that in America the true strength of the country lies far more in the State governments than in the Federal government. The Federal judges are aware of the relative weakness of the power in whose name they act. They are readier to give up a claim of jurisdiction that is rightfully theirs than to press a privilege they have no legal title to.
Different Cases of Jurisdiction

The matter and the party are the first conditions of Federal jurisdiction — Suits in which ambassadors are involved — Suits of the Union — Of a separate State — By whom tried — Cases arising from the laws of the Union — Why they are judged by the Federal tribunals — Cases concerning the performance of contracts tried by the Federal courts — Consequence of this arrangement.

Having provided the means of fixing the competence of the Federal courts, the legislators of the Union defined the cases that should fall within their jurisdiction. They established, on the one hand, that certain parties must always be brought before the Federal courts, whatever the special nature of the case; and, on the other, that certain kinds of cases must always be brought before those same courts, whatever the standing of the parties to the suit. These distinctions were thus accepted as the basis of Federal jurisdiction.

Ambassadors are the representatives of nations at peace with the Union, and whatever concerns them concerns the whole Union to some degree. When an ambassador is a party to a suit, the suit affects the welfare of the nation, and it is natural that a Federal tribunal should be called on to decide it.

The Union itself may be sued or may bring a suit. In that case, to take the matter to a tribunal of any other sovereignty than its own would go against the usage of every nation and against common sense. So the Federal courts hear these affairs.

Suppose two parties from two different States are at law with each other. It would hardly be fitting to try the case before a court of either State. The safest remedy is a tribunal like that of the Union, which neither party can distrust, and which is the most natural as well as the most reliable choice.

When the parties are not private persons but States, a weighty political concern joins the same motive of fairness. The rank of the parties lends national importance to all their quarrels, and even the pettiest lawsuit between States may be said to touch the peace of the whole Union. *f

f [ The Constitution also says that the Federal courts shall decide “controversies between a State and the citizens of another State.” Here a most important constitutional question arose: whether the jurisdiction given by the Constitution in cases where a State is a party extended to suits brought against a State as well as by it, or was confined exclusively to the latter. The question was examined at great length in the case of Chisholm v. Georgia, and the majority of the Supreme Court decided it in the affirmative. The decision caused general alarm among the States, and an amendment was proposed and ratified that removed the power entirely, as far as suits brought against a State are concerned.
